newsitem.title: TURKEY: Scattered clashes mar Turkish May Day protests.
newsitem.headline: Scattered clashes mar Turkish May Day protests.

text.p: Scattered clashes marred protests by tens of thousands of Turks in a May Day march on Thursday at which leftist demonstrators accused the Islamist-led government of links to a security scandal.
"Money for health, not for the gangs," and "Money for education, not for the gangs," chanted marchers in Istanbul.

A scandal erupted last year after a car crash in the town of Susurluk in which a top policeman and a wanted mobster died. It has led to allegations that the state used right-wing gangs to kill left-wing and Kurdish political opponents.
At least 10 protesters were injured when police clashed with one group of leftist demonstrators after security officials had stopped them marching towards the city centre, witnesses said.
Two people were hurt in a separate incident when fights broke out between rival masked left-wing groups and one marcher was taken away by ambulance, witnesses said.

One group, many wearing red bandanas to cover their faces, attacked their rivals with sticks and wooden planks in a pitched battle along an Istanbul highway. The others responded with taunts and volleys of stones.
May Day protests in Turkey have a history of violence.
Security was tight security in Istanbul after the deaths of three people in May Day rioting last year, when damage amounted to $2 million.

Twelve thousand policemen backed by more than 2,000 soldiers were on duty. Heavily armed gendarmerie forces and so-called "robocops" -- police with plastic body armour -- cordoned off Abide-i Hurriyet Square with armoured cars.
Marchers were searched entering the square and a police helicopter circled.
Around 1,500 regular army commandos, backed by armoured personnel carriers, were on stand-by alert at a football stadium near the rally.
Earlier in the day, trade union leaders laid a wreath of red carnations in Istanbul's main Taksim Square in memory of 37 people killed at a May Day rally there 20 years ago.

No one was ever charged for the deaths on May Day, 1977, when a suspected rightist gunman fired on protesters from a building above the square. Most of the victims were crushed to death in the resulting stampede.

"Twenty years ago today, 37 workers died in this place. It has now become clear that their killers were the gangs within the state which came out into the open with the events of Susurluk," said labour leader Kemal Daysal in reference to the security scandal.
The affair has damaged the standing of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, now embroiled in a bitter row with the secularist army over the role of religion.
About a dozen people from the tiny Revolutionary Labour party were later arrested in Taksim Square shouting: "Revolution or death."
The marchers were also protesting about deteriorating conditions for workers in Turkey.
A report in the daily Sabah newspaper said on Thursday that workers' wages had risen well below the rate of inflation since 1990.
About 10,000 people took to the streets of Ankara and about 4,000 protested in Diyarbakir, the biggest city in the mainly Kurdish southeast.
